article.title: Why an Average Can Hide Two Very Different Groups
article.why: A simple introduction to composition effects in business data.

paragraphs.en:
Averages are useful because they turn many numbers into one simple number. But an average can also hide important differences inside a group. Imagine two stores. Store A has ten customers: five spend $10 and five spend $90. Store B also has ten customers, and every customer spends $50. The average spending is $50 in both stores. If we only look at the average, the stores seem the same. In reality, their customers behave very differently.

This matters in business analysis. Suppose the average annual spending of members rises from $400 to $450. It is tempting to say that customers are spending more. However, perhaps low-spending members left the service while high-spending members stayed. The behavior of each remaining customer may not have changed at all. The average increased because the mix of customers changed.

The same problem appears when comparing regions, age groups, products, or years. A company may report that average salary increased, but the increase may partly come from hiring more senior employees. A hospital may report a longer average stay because it treated more serious cases. An app may report higher average revenue per user after many free users became inactive. In each case, the average is correct, but the story behind it may be different from the first impression.

A good analyst therefore asks two questions. First, did values change inside the groups? Second, did the size of the groups change? It helps to compare the average with the median, percentiles, distributions, and segment-level results. A chart can also reveal whether one group contains two very different populations.

The lesson is simple: an average describes a population, not a typical person in every situation. Before saying that customers became richer, more active, or more valuable, check whether individual behavior changed or whether the population mix changed. One extra breakdown can prevent a misleading conclusion.

A single summary number can hide differences between customer groups.
The customer mix changed even though individual behavior did not.

business.term: Break the average down by segment before interpreting the movement.
